title: Reminiscing, Praying and Caring
keywords: Pray as though everything depended on God
primary_topics: Commencement address to 250 graduates of the FEU-Nicanor Reyes Medical Foundation, delivered January 28, 2022
Two pieces of advice: (1) Always pray and trust God; (2) Work with competence and care -- encapsulated in 'Pray as though everything depended on God; work as though everything depended on you'

Personal near-death narrative: dysentery in wartime Pampanga (age 6), ruptured appendix at FEU Hospital (law student), six-by-six truck incident in Sampaloc, multiple other health crises -- all survived through divine providence
The ruptured appendix story as both a comic reversal (the anti-fee student who had to pay the fee) and an illustration of Filipino doctors' superior care and compassion
sub_topics: Relationship with President Antonio H. Abad Jr.: close friend and compadre for 60+ years; law partners at PABLAW (Panganiban, Abad and Associates Law Office, formed 1965); godfather to Abad's daughter Anna Maria 'ADA' Abad (expert in labor law, law dean of Adamson, managing partner of their firm)

CJP's FEU background: law student 1956-1960; CSO President 1957-1958 (sophomore); over 36,000 FEU students; vigorously opposed the compulsory P6.00 health and hospitalization fee as not universally beneficial

The ruptured appendix story: 1958 stomach ache during evening classes at FEU Institute of Law; rushed to FEU Hospital on Morayta Street (now Nicanor Reyes Sr. Street); Dr. Ricardo Alfonso (medical director, renowned surgeon) recognized CJP and offered a choice -- pay full bills or pay the six-peso fee; CJP surrendered: 'Doctor, you win. I will withdraw my opposition'; surgery revealed ruptured appendix at the rear left (unusual position) contained by fat

The prior episode explaining the rupture: two weeks earlier, CJP was with ~300 student leaders touring Mayon Volcano after NUSP Seminar in Naga City; severe stomach ache; rushed to only open clinic at the foot of Mayon -- St. Mary's Maternity Clinic in Tabaco, Albay; attending doctor thought indigestion and gave castor oil (vomited immediately); then injected morphine; CJP slept 24 hours; woke up pain-free; commuted to Naga for dance party

Childhood near-death: dysentery at age 6 in barrio of Candaba, Pampanga during World War II; Japanese occupation; no hospital, medicine, doctor or nurse; given up for dead; mother watched over him until miraculous recovery

Other health crises: 1983 diabetes diagnosis (still managed by Dr. Augusto Litonjua, seen every 3 months); three operations for recurring hemorrhoids; failed ECG, 2D Echocardiography, and treadmill stress tests; passed angiogram (Dr. Dante Morales: rare natural skip in heartbeat, arteries okay); almost run over by army six-by-six truck in 1949 while peddling newspapers from jeepney on España Street -- jumped, fell flat, truck passed over his lean body with enough clearance
Theological explanation for survival: CJP attributes all near-death escapes to the Lord Jesus Christ and the Blessed Mother Mary -- 'probably because I have not accomplished His mission for me'
Isaiah 55:8-10 quoted in full as the foundation for the first advice: 'my thoughts are not your thoughts, and my ways are not your ways'

The FEU Prayer and its connection to the Centennial Prayer of the Courts (composed 2001, still recited in all courts today): 'Direct, O God, we beseech Thee all our actions by Thy holy inspiration...' -- CJP so loved this prayer that it became a basis for the centenary prayer drafted from a CJ Davide Jr. draft

Filipino doctor example: Dr. Horatio 'Cabby' Cabasares migrated to Perry, Georgia (pop. 19,000) in 1973; served with Pinoy caring and empathy; died of COVID-19 December 16, 2020; honored with a bronze plaque: 'Dr. Cabby's cheerful smile, caring heart, and encouraging words will not be forgotten'

Contrasting American hospital story: an unnamed Filipino billionaire (head of a major conglomerate, now deceased) confined in Houston, Texas for heart bypass and kidney transplant; regretted going to the US because American doctors treated him as 'an object to be studied, operated on and monitored' -- not as a human being with fear, loneliness and desperation

stances.claim: Prayer should not be a petition for God to remove difficulties but for God to grant the strength and will to overcome them -- 'God will always be there to help us, to strengthen us and to enable us to live healthily, happily and mightily -- in His own way, in His own time, not in our way, not in our time' (Isaiah 55:8-10 as the anchor).
stances.rhetorical_move: reframing of prayer from petition-for-removal to petition-for-strength -- a substantive theological distinction
stances.confidence: asserted as personal credo with scriptural grounding

stances.claim: Filipino doctors and nurses outperform American medical facilities in the dimension that matters most to patients: care, compassion, and treating patients as human beings with fear, loneliness and desperation -- not merely as objects to be studied and operated on. The contrasting testimonies of the Houston billionaire and Dr. Cabasares of Perry, Georgia together prove this.
stances.rhetorical_move: two-witness comparative argument: one Filipino patient in America (negative) and one Filipino doctor in America (positive) -- establishing the Filipino 'care advantage'

notable_anecdotes: The ruptured appendix comedy: CJP had vigorously opposed FEU's compulsory P6 health fee as not universally beneficial. In 1958, he was rushed to FEU Hospital with a terrible stomach ache. Dr. Ricardo Alfonso -- who knew CJP from his fee opposition -- offered him a choice: pay full bills plus professional fees, or pay the six-peso fee. 'I softly replied amid my indescribably wrenching pain: Doctor, you win. I will withdraw my opposition to the six-peso medical bill.' Surgery revealed a ruptured appendix -- at the rear left, unusual position -- contained by fat.

The prior Mayon episode: two weeks before the appendix surgery, CJP had a terrible stomach ache while touring Mayon Volcano with ~300 student leaders after a NUSP Seminar in Naga City. Rushed to the only open clinic at the foot of Mayon -- St. Mary's Maternity Clinic in Tabaco, Albay. All other patients were there for labor pains; CJP's pain was also abdominal -- just not a baby. Doctor gave castor oil (immediately vomited), then morphine injection; CJP slept 24 hours, woke up pain-free, and commuted back to Naga for the closing dance party.

The six-by-six truck survival: in 1949, the nine-year-old CJP was peddling newspapers while riding the rear of a speeding jeepney on España Street, Sampaloc. He jumped off, lost his balance, fell flat on the cemented road. An oncoming army six-by-six truck passed directly over him -- but its road clearance was just enough for his 'lean and thin body to slide under its axles and escape serious injury and death.'

World War II dysentery: at age 6, in a barrio of Candaba, Pampanga, with Japanese forces occupying the country, no hospital, no medicine, no doctor or nurse available. 'He was given up for dead. But my mother did not surrender. She watched over me as I miraculously recovered in her arms.'

Dr. Horatio 'Cabby' Cabasares: migrated to Perry, Georgia (pop. 19,000) in 1973; served with Filipino caring, sincerity, empathy and affection; died of COVID-19, December 16, 2020. Bronze plaque at the hospital: 'Dr. Cabby's cheerful smile, caring heart, and encouraging words will not be forgotten, and his faithful dedication to others will continue to inspire the community for years to come.'

The Houston billionaire: an unnamed Filipino who headed one of the biggest conglomerates, confined in a Houston hospital for heart bypass and kidney transplant. 'He regretted having gone to the USA... American doctors and nurses viewed him merely an object to be studied, to be operated on and to be monitored... He longed for the companionship, care and love of Filipino doctors, nurses and other professionals.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 28, 2022 as the commencement address to 250 FEU-NRMF graduates, this speech by CJP -- who acknowledges he normally declines speaking invitations at age 85 but could not refuse his compadre and 60-year friend President Antonio Abad Jr. -- is built around two pieces of advice: always pray and trust God, and work with competence and care. The first is illustrated by a cumulative near-death inventory: dysentery at age 6 in wartime Candaba, Pampanga (no hospital, no medicine, given up for dead, revived in his mother's arms); a severe stomach ache touring Mayon Volcano in 1958 misdiagnosed as indigestion at a maternity clinic (treated with castor oil and morphine, slept 24 hours, woke up pain-free and attended the dance party); two weeks later, the same pain recurred at FEU law school and he was rushed to FEU Hospital where Dr. Ricardo Alfonso -- knowing CJP as the vocal opponent of the compulsory P6 medical fee -- offered him a choice between full billing and the six-peso fee; CJP surrendered: 'Doctor, you win. I will withdraw my opposition.' Surgery revealed a ruptured appendix, unusually at the rear left, contained by fat; he also survived being run over by a six-by-six truck in 1949 as a nine-year-old newspaper peddler on España Street, whose clearance was just enough for his 'lean and thin body to slide under its axles.' He attributes all escapes to divine providence (Isaiah 55:8-10: 'my thoughts are not your thoughts, my ways are not your ways') and traces his own prayer life to FEU chaplain Fr. Michael Nolan's four basic prayers -- including the FEU Prayer that became the basis of the Centennial Prayer of the Courts (2001, still recited in all courts today). The second advice, care, is illustrated by two contrasting witnesses: an unnamed Filipino billionaire who regretted his Houston heart-bypass hospitalization where American doctors treated him as 'an object to be studied' rather than 'a human being with emotions of fear, loneliness and desperation'; and Dr. Horatio 'Cabby' Cabasares, who served Perry, Georgia (pop. 19,000) with Filipino caring and empathy from 1973 until his COVID-19 death on December 16, 2020, honored with a bronze plaque. CJP closes: 'Pray as though everything depended on God; work as though everything depended on you.'
